## Natural history notes

A medium-sized blister beetle characterized by a soft, elongated body, narrow head, long legs, and dark gray to blackish coloration, with males having distinctive twisted or modified antennae that give the species its common name. In Florida, the Twisted-horn Epicauta is found in open and semi-open habitats such as fields, roadsides, pastures, pine flatwoods, gardens, and weedy edges where flowers and herbaceous plants occur. Adults feed on flowers and foliage and should not be handled because blister beetles can release cantharidin, a defensive chemical that may irritate skin, while the larvae develop in soil and typically feed on grasshopper eggs or other buried insect resources.
